newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African capital paralysed by mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Central African capital paralysed by mutiny.

text.p: Rebel soldiers and loyalist troops on Tuesday fought gunbattles on the streets of the Central African Republic capital, where shops and businesses have closed and districts have divided into competing areas of control.
A two-week-old mutiny, the country's third this year, has shifted from grievances over pay and status to rebel demands for the resignation of elected President Ange-Felix Patasse.
Rebels reiterated on Tuesday they would not return to the barracks until they have disarmed civilians and African mercenaries from Chad and Sudan backing Patasse.
"The president is the cause of tribal hatred," rebel spokesman Captain Anicet Saulet told BBC French service radio.
"We will press on with the disarming of civilians and the militias that have been formed. We want all foreign troops to leave," he said.
The mutiny has divided the city into a rebel-held south and west, and a northern and central area controlled by loyalists or French troops based in Bangui under bilateral accords.
The population is split on tribal lines, with Yakomas, who are prominent the army, hunted in pro-Patasse districts.
Patasse's spokesman Prosper Douba accused rebels of holding the entire population hostage and of staging a coup d'etat.
"It is a coup d'etat, pure and simple," Douba told the BBC. "They want to overthrow a government elected democratically by the Central African people and take its place."
On Monday Patasse's supporters put up roadblocks in their bastions of the capital and residents said pro-Patasse militants seized at least four Yakoma hostages.
Witnesses said barricades mounted by members of Patasse's Baya tribe went up in the Combatants area and Sarra. Militants looking for Yakomas checked residents' identities.
Roadblocks also appeared on roads into rebel strongholds.
Hospital sources said at least seven people, all civilians, had been killed since the start of the revolt on November 16.
Patasse decreed a night curfew on Bangui on Saturday and repeated his call on mutineers to lay down their weapons unconditionally.
Parliamentary sources said all the country's 23 political parties had been summoned to a crisis meeting at the National Assembly on Tuesday.

Talks were also planned between the rebels and an eight-party opposition alliance which has luanched a new mediation. Church-brokered talks broke down after rebels stood their ground in their demand for Patasse's resignation.
French troops who helped put down a more serious mutiny in May are protecting Patasse and key points in the city but have not clashed with rebels.
